reviews.error: Response was not a usable review; this reviewer's output was lost

findings.title: relaxedEdgeDensity crashes if Map key lookup returns undefined
findings.description: The expression `indexes.get(groups[i]!)!` uses a non-null assertion on the Map lookup result. The `indexes` map is built from the original `groups` array in `agreementClusters` using array elements as keys. However, `splitCompatibleChains` creates new sub-arrays, and `connectedComponents` maps indexes back to `groups[index]!`. The `indexes` map is constructed with the *original* group array references as keys. If `relaxedEdgeDensity` is called with `component` arrays whose inner `TaggedFinding[]` references are the same objects from `groups`, this works. But if any code path ever creates new array wrappers (e.g., via spread or slice), the Map lookup returns `undefined`, the `!` assertion hides the `undefined`, and `.has()` throws a runtime TypeError. The same pattern applies to `indexes.get(groups[j]!)!`. This is fragile and depends on referential identity being preserved through all code paths.
findings.suggestedFix: Either add a guard: `const idxI = indexes.get(groups[i]!); const idxJ = indexes.get(groups[j]!); if (idxI === undefined || idxJ === undefined) continue;` or restructure to pass indices directly rather than relying on object identity in a Map.

findings.title: Louvain community detection may not converge or may oscillate
findings.description: The `relaxedCommunities` function implements a simplified weighted Louvain. The pass limit is `Math.min(count * 2, 20)`, but the `moved` flag only breaks when no node changes community in a full pass. However, the gain comparison uses `Number.EPSILON` which is extremely small (~2.2e-16). For floating-point weights in the range [0,1], rounding differences can cause oscillation between communities where gains differ by less than EPSILON in one pass but more in the next (due to `communityDegrees` being mutated in-place during the same pass). The tie-breaking rule `candidate < best` helps but doesn't fully prevent oscillation when a node is moved to community A, then community B's degree changes, making B preferable next pass, etc. Consider using a larger epsilon (like the existing `CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON = 1e-9`) or computing gains against a snapshot of community degrees per pass.
findings.suggestedFix: Use `CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON` (1e-9) instead of `Number.EPSILON` for the gain comparison, or snapshot `communityDegrees` at the start of each pass to avoid in-pass mutations affecting gain calculations.

findings.title: communityDegrees mutated before gain evaluation creates asymmetric removal
findings.description: The line `communityDegrees[current] -= degrees[index]!` removes the node's degree from its current community before evaluating all candidates. However, when evaluating the gain for re-inserting into `current`, the `communityDegrees[current]` has already been decremented. This is correct for the standard Louvain first phase. But the `bestGain` initialization computes the gain for staying in `current` using the *already-decremented* `communityDegrees[current]`, while the loop over `candidates` also includes `current`. This means the gain for `current` is computed twice with the same value (redundant but not wrong). More importantly, if `best` remains `current`, the line `communityDegrees[best] += degrees[index]!` restores it correctly. However, if the node was degree 0, it's skipped, so this is fine. The real issue: if `best !== current`, the node's degree is added to `best` but was already removed from `current` — correct. But if in a subsequent iteration within the same pass, another node evaluates community `current`, it sees the reduced degree. This is the standard in-pass mutation behavior of Louvain but can lead to order-dependent results.
findings.suggestedFix: Document that results are pass-order dependent, or snapshot communityDegrees per pass for determinism.

findings.title: mergeAnchoredCommunities has O(n²) splice+sort in a while loop
findings.description: The `mergeAnchoredCommunities` function uses `remaining.splice(j, 1)` followed by `remaining.sort(compareAgreementClusters)` inside a nested loop with a `while(merged)` outer loop. Each merge triggers a full re-sort of the remaining array. In the worst case with many merges, this becomes O(n² log n). For typical corpus sizes this is likely fine, but for large inputs it could be a performance concern. Additionally, after `splice` and `break outer`, the `while` loop restarts from `i=0`, re-examining already-checked pairs.
findings.suggestedFix: For large inputs, consider using a priority queue or only re-sorting affected elements. For typical sizes, add a comment noting the expected input bounds.

findings.title: Cross-edge check in mergeAnchoredCommunities may miss valid merges
findings.description: The `hasCrossEdge` check requires that a relaxed edge exists between two members with *different* `model::role` assignments. However, `relaxedLocationWeight` returns 0 if `relaxedLocationDuplicate` returns false, which itself requires `compatibleClaimKinds` to pass. If two communities discuss the same defect but use incompatible claim-kind vocabulary (e.g., one mentions 'missing index' triggering `PERFORMANCE_CONTRACT_PATTERN` and the other doesn't), the cross-edge will be 0 and the merge is blocked even though anchors strongly agree. This could cause under-merging in edge cases where the claim-kind patterns are too aggressive.
findings.suggestedFix: Consider whether the cross-edge check should use a relaxed version of compatibility, or whether anchor agreement with sufficient support (e.g., 3+ shared anchors) should be sufficient without requiring a cross-edge.

findings.title: corroborationFieldSimilar returns true for two shared underscore tokens
findings.description: The function returns true if `shared.some(token => !token.includes('_'))` OR `shared.length >= 2`. This means two findings sharing only two code identifiers (e.g., `trigger_label` and `column_name`) will pass the field-similarity check, even though the comment above says 'A shared code identifier alone is only evidence that findings discuss the same function, not the same defect.' Two identifiers from the same function could still create false edges between different defects in that function.
findings.suggestedFix: Consider requiring at least one non-underscore token, or requiring `shared.length >= 3` for the all-underscore case.

findings.title: relaxedLocationWeight weights sum to 1.0 but description may be undefined
findings.description: The weight formula uses `nonEmptyFieldSimilarity(a.description, b.description) * 0.2` and `nonEmptyFieldSimilarity(a.suggestedFix, b.suggestedFix) * 0.55`. If both description and suggestedFix are empty/undefined for both findings, these terms contribute 0, and the weight is purely title-based (max 0.25). This means a match can pass `relaxedLocationDuplicate` (which requires detail similarity >= 0.1) but then get a very low weight. However, `relaxedLocationDuplicate` already gates on detail similarity, so `relaxedLocationWeight` returning >0 implies detail similarity was met. The inconsistency is that the weight formula gives 55% weight to `suggestedFix` but the gate in `relaxedLocationDuplicate` uses `Math.max(descriptionSimilarity, fixSimilarity)`, meaning a match could pass the gate on description alone but get a low weight because fix similarity is 0. This is by design but worth noting.
findings.suggestedFix: No code change needed, but consider adding a comment explaining the intentional asymmetry between the gate and the weight formula.

findings.title: CORROBORATION_STOPWORDS extends STOPWORDS with common code-review terms
findings.description: The stopword list includes very generic terms like 'code', 'function', 'issue', 'test', 'tests', 'config', 'file', 'files'. While these reduce noise, they could also remove meaningful signal in contexts where the finding is specifically about configuration files vs. source files, or about test files vs. implementation files. For example, two findings about 'test configuration' vs 'source configuration' would lose the distinguishing 'config' token.
findings.suggestedFix: Consider whether domain-specific terms like 'config' and 'test' should be stopworded, or whether they carry enough semantic weight to keep. At minimum, add a comment explaining why these specific terms were chosen.

findings.title: Regex patterns for claim-kind compatibility are fragile
findings.description: The patterns `TYPE_CONTRACT_PATTERN`, `PERFORMANCE_CONTRACT_PATTERN`, `DATA_TYPE_CONTRACT_PATTERN`, and `GLOBAL_LOG_CAPTURE_PATTERN` use regex matching on titles. The `DATA_TYPE_CONTRACT_PATTERN` includes `\bcast(?:ing)?\b` which would match any title containing the word 'cast' or 'casting', including 'broadcast', 'forecast', or 'podcast'. The `\b` word boundary should prevent 'broadcast' but 'cast' is a common English word that could appear in non-type-related contexts (e.g., 'cast a wider net').
findings.suggestedFix: Consider using more specific patterns like `\btype cast(?:ing)?\b` or `\bexplicit cast\b` to reduce false positives.

findings.title: attachmentEvidence anchor count check may incorrectly reject valid attachments
findings.description: The condition `if (anchorCount < 2 && !(anchorCount === 1 && fixSupport >= 2))` returns early with zero support. This means: if anchorCount is 0, always reject (correct). If anchorCount is 1, only proceed if fixSupport >= 2. But `fixSupport` is computed by checking `nonEmptyFieldSimilarity(singleton.finding.suggestedFix, member.finding.suggestedFix) >= CORROBORATED_DETAIL_THRESHOLD` across cluster members. If the singleton's `suggestedFix` is undefined/empty, `nonEmptyFieldSimilarity` returns 0 for all comparisons, making `fixSupport` always 0, and the function returns early even if the singleton has strong title/description alignment with the cluster.
findings.suggestedFix: Consider also checking description similarity as a fallback when suggestedFix is empty, or adjust the early-return condition to account for missing suggestedFix.

findings.title: Attachment loop bound uses clusters.length which changes during iteration
findings.description: The outer loop `for (let round = 0; round < Math.min(clusters.length, CORROBORATED_MAX_ATTACHMENT_ROUNDS); round++)` uses `clusters.length` as an upper bound. However, `clusters.length` doesn't change during the loop (clusters are emptied via `candidate.groups = []` but not removed from the array). The `Math.min` with `CORROBORATED_MAX_ATTACHMENT_ROUNDS` (2) bounds it correctly. But the `clusters.filter(cluster => cluster.groups.length > 0)` at line ~920 is needed to clean up emptied clusters. This is correct but the loop bound comment could be clearer.
findings.suggestedFix: No code change needed. Consider a comment clarifying that clusters.length is stable and the real bound is CORROBORATED_MAX_ATTACHMENT_ROUNDS.

findings.title: Tie-breaking in attachment ranking may be too strict
findings.description: The tie-breaking condition requires `ranked[0]!.support === ranked[1].support && Math.abs(ranked[0]!.strength - ranked[1].strength) <= CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON && ranked[0]!.size === ranked[1].size` to skip the attachment. `CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON` is 1e-9, which is extremely tight for floating-point strength values that are sums of similarity scores. Two clusters with strengths differing by 1e-8 would not be considered tied, potentially leading to arbitrary attachments based on floating-point noise.
findings.suggestedFix: Consider using a larger epsilon like 0.01 or 0.001 for strength comparison, or document that 1e-9 is intentionally strict.

findings.title: Test fixtures use hardcoded finding data without verifying similarity assumptions
findings.description: The test asserts `expect(combinedSimilarity(variants[0]!, variants[1]!)).toBeLessThan(0.3)` to verify the findings are below the normal dedup threshold. However, the three variant findings are constructed with very similar titles (all mention 'icon', 'name', 'match/prefix'). If the `combinedSimilarity` function or `jaccardSimilarity` is later modified, this precondition assertion might fail, breaking the test for the wrong reason. More importantly, there's no test verifying that the findings *would* be merged by the corroborated path specifically (i.e., that `relaxedLocationDuplicate` returns true for them).
findings.suggestedFix: Add a direct unit test for `relaxedLocationDuplicate` with these variants to verify the relaxed path triggers. Also consider testing with findings that are clearly above the normal threshold to ensure the corroborated path doesn't interfere with normal dedup.

findings.title: Missing edge case tests for corroborated clustering
findings.description: The test suite covers the happy path (3 models merge), the two-model rejection, claim-kind separation, and determinism. Missing edge cases include: (1) empty input to `mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters`, (2) a single finding (no possible corroboration), (3) findings with empty/undefined descriptions and suggestedFix, (4) findings at the exact boundary of `lineWindow`, (5) findings with opposing sentiment that should not merge, (6) more than CORROBORATED_MAX_ATTACHMENT_ROUNDS rounds needed, (7) all findings from the same model::role (should not corroborate), (8) findings in different files that share location lines.
findings.suggestedFix: Add tests for: single finding input, empty description/suggestedFix fields, boundary lineWindow values, opposing sentiment blocking, same-model-multiple-roles not counting as distinct reviewers, and cross-file rejection.

findings.title: Determinism test only checks reversed order, not arbitrary permutations
findings.description: The determinism test reverses the review array and checks the output signature matches. However, with 3 elements, there are 6 permutations. Reversal only tests one specific reordering. A more thorough test would check multiple random permutations or all permutations for small inputs.
findings.suggestedFix: For 3 elements, test all 6 permutations: `const perms = [[0,1,2],[0,2,1],[1,0,2],[1,2,0],[2,0,1],[2,1,0]]; for (const perm of perms) { expect(signature(perm.map(i => reviews[i]))).toEqual(signature(reviews)); }`

findings.title: miningProxyOvermerged test throws Error for missing mustStaySeparate
findings.description: When `c.expected.miningProxyOvermerged` is true but `mustStaySeparate` is undefined, the test throws a raw `Error` with a message. This is a test-fixture validation check, but using `throw new Error` inside a test body is unusual. It would be clearer to use a `beforeAll` or `beforeEach` validation, or to use `expect(...).toBeDefined()` with a descriptive message. Also, the `continue` statement after the two `it` blocks means the normal merge test is skipped for overmerged cases, which is correct but subtle.
findings.suggestedFix: Consider using `expect(c.expected.mustStaySeparate).toBeDefined()` as a guard, or validate the corpus structure in a `beforeAll` block.

findings.title: Consensus score check uses division that could be misleading
findings.description: The test checks `pairs.size / c.expected.successfulReviews < DEFAULT_THRESHOLDS.minConsensusScore` to verify separated concepts are below threshold. However, `pairs.size` counts distinct `model::role` strings in the group, while `successfulReviews` is the total number of reviews. If a group has members from the same model::role pair, `pairs.size` undercounts. The test assumes each member has a unique model::role, which may not always hold after the new merging logic combines groups.
findings.suggestedFix: Verify that the denominator should be `successfulReviews` or the actual number of reviews that produced findings in this group. Add a comment explaining the expected relationship.

findings.title: connectedComponents inner function captures mutable inCore and adjacency
findings.description: The `connectedComponents` function is defined inside `agreementClusters` and captures `inCore`, `adjacency`, and `groups` from the enclosing scope. It's called twice: once with `wantedCore=true` and once with `wantedCore=false`. Between these calls, `adjacency` is mutated (edges between different communities are removed at lines ~740-743). This is intentional but the mutation happens before both calls, so both calls see the pruned adjacency. The 2-core peeling also mutates `degree` and `inCore`. This is correct but makes the function hard to reason about and test in isolation.
findings.suggestedFix: Consider extracting `connectedComponents` to a standalone function that takes explicit parameters, or add a detailed comment about the mutation ordering.

findings.title: collapseSameReviewer called twice on potentially merged groups
findings.description: In the original code, `collapseSameReviewer` was called once per coherent group. In the new code, `mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters` may merge multiple strict groups, and then `collapseSameReviewer` is called again on the merged result at line ~1040. If `collapseSameReviewer` is not idempotent or if the merged group contains findings that were already collapsed, this could produce unexpected results. Specifically, if two strict groups each had their same-reviewer findings collapsed, and then the groups are merged, the merged group might have findings from the same reviewer that weren't collapsed together in the first pass.
findings.suggestedFix: Verify that `collapseSameReviewer` is idempotent and handles the case where input already contains collapsed groups. The second call at line ~1040 should handle this correctly if it processes all members, but add a test for this scenario.

findings.title: Two-reviewer rejection test doesn't verify the strict path still works
findings.description: The test 'does not treat only two reviewer assignments as corroboration' verifies that two findings from two different models remain separate. However, it doesn't verify that these findings would also fail the normal (strict) dedup path. If the findings happen to be similar enough for strict dedup, the test would pass for the wrong reason (they'd be merged by strict dedup, then the test would fail). The test should also assert that `combinedSimilarity` is below the strict threshold, similar to the first test.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `expect(combinedSimilarity(variants[0]!, variants[1]!)).toBeLessThan(jaccardThreshold)` to verify the findings are below the strict threshold and the test is specifically exercising the corroborated path rejection.

findings.title: Interpolating optional description string produces false 'undefined' anchor tokens
findings.description: In `attachmentEvidence`, `${singleton.finding.description}` is interpolated directly into a template literal. If `description` is `undefined`, JS template string conversion converts it to the literal string `"undefined"`. `corroborationTokens` then extracts `"undefined"` as a token because it is longer than 1 character and not present in `CORROBORATION_STOPWORDS`. As a result, any findings with undefined descriptions will falsely share `'undefined'` as a semantic anchor token.
findings.suggestedFix: `${singleton.finding.title} ${singleton.finding.description ?? ''} ${singleton.finding.suggestedFix ?? ''}`

findings.title: Incomplete sort comparator in splitCompatibleChains can lead to non-deterministic results
findings.description: The sort comparator in `splitCompatibleChains` compares `file`, `startLine`, `endLine`, and `title`. When two findings share identical values for these four fields, the comparator returns `0`. Because array sorting preserves input relative order for equal elements, the order of clusters depends on the initial ordering of `component`. If input reviews arrive in a different order, the resulting cluster chains may differ.
findings.suggestedFix:
return left.file.localeCompare(right.file) ||
  left.startLine - right.startLine ||
  left.endLine - right.endLine ||
  left.title.localeCompare(right.title) ||
  left.id.localeCompare(right.id);

findings.title: Domain-specific claim heuristics embedded in generic deduper
findings.description: compatibleClaimKinds hardcodes production-corpus patterns (Elixir @spec/typespec, N+1/unbounded query, global log capture) directly into the shared consensus dedup path. That couples a generic clustering module to particular ecosystems and to RCL-17 incident wording; new false merges/splits will require code changes instead of configuration or pluggable classifiers, and unrelated repos inherit Elixir/log-capture special cases.
findings.suggestedFix: Move claim-kind signals behind a data-driven strategy (config, taxonomy tags on findings, or an injectable ClaimKindClassifier). Keep the deduper responsible only for “kinds must be compatible,” not for the specific regex inventory.

findings.title: Large corroborated-clustering algorithm added to an already dense module
findings.description: Roughly 600 lines of weighted Louvain, 2-core peeling, anchor merging, and fringe attachment were inlined into deduper.ts. This concentrates multiple independent algorithms, constants, and graph mutations in one module, making boundary testing hard (communities vs attachment vs claim filters) and increasing regression risk when tuning one stage.
findings.suggestedFix: Extract a dedicated module (e.g. corroboratedLocationClusters.ts) exporting mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters plus pure helpers (relaxedCommunities, agreementClusters, attachmentEvidence). Add focused unit tests per stage with fixture graphs.

findings.title: Louvain pass is only phase-1 local moving
findings.description: relaxedCommunities runs a bounded first-phase weighted Louvain (local label moves) without the aggregation/second phase or community-id compression. Abandoned community labels can remain as empty attractors, and partitions can stop at a coarser local optimum. For corroboration boundaries this may under-merge communities that a full Louvain pass would join, leaving true duplicates split unless later anchor/attachment stages compensate.
findings.suggestedFix: Either rename/document this as “modularity-greedy local moving” (not full Louvain), or add an aggregation phase and relabel communities to dense ids after each pass. Add graph fixtures where phase-1 alone fails but full Louvain succeeds.

findings.title: CORROBORATED_MIN_DENSITY is nearly inert under 2-core
findings.description: Corroboration requires a 2-core of the relaxed graph. In a simple undirected graph every 2-core has minimum degree ≥ 2, so any core with ≥3 nodes already has edge density ≥ 2/n and typically well above 0.2 (a 3-node core must be a triangle, density 1). Combined with CORROBORATED_MIN_REVIEWERS = 3, the density threshold rarely rejects anything the 2-core did not already reject, which makes the constant misleading as a tunable over-merge control.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the density check, or redefine density after peeling using only core-induced edges and calibrate it on graphs that can fail it (or switch to a stronger structural metric such as average edge weight or conductance).

findings.title: Negative corpus case still carries positive-merge expectations
findings.description: ao-7467-r1 sets miningProxyOvermerged/mustStaySeparate but still leaves clearsThresholdIfMerged: true, agreementRatioIfMerged: 0.444, and mixed memberTitles from both concepts. undermerge-corpus.test.ts skips the merge assertions when the flag is set, so the stale fields are dead and contradictory documentation for anyone reading the fixture alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Clear or rewrite positive-merge fields for the negative case (e.g. clearsThresholdIfMerged: false, agreementRatioIfMerged: null, memberTitles split per concept or removed) so the fixture is self-consistent.

findings.title: Secondary negative test locks both concepts below threshold
findings.description: The test titled “separated concepts retain their independent agreement” actually asserts each separated group’s reviewer-pair ratio is strictly below DEFAULT_THRESHOLDS.minConsensusScore. That freezes “both concepts are unactionable when split” rather than only “they must not share a group.” If fixture membership is later corrected so one real concept legitimately clears consensus, this assertion fails even though separation is correct. It also uses DEFAULT_THRESHOLDS instead of c.expected.minConsensusScore.
findings.suggestedFix: Keep the mustStaySeparate identity assertion as the primary guard. If you need a score check, assert against c.expected and document expected per-concept ratios explicitly, or assert only that the over-merged combined group does not appear—not that both sides stay forever below threshold.

findings.title: Heavy non-null assertions on Map/array lookups
findings.description: relaxedEdgeDensity and the graph construction path repeatedly use indexes.get(...)! and adjacency[i]! without narrowing. Reference-keyed Maps are correct only while callers pass the original group object identities; a future transform that copies inner groups would turn these into runtime undefined index accesses.
findings.suggestedFix: Helper getters that throw descriptive errors on missing index/edge entries, or store numeric ids on groups up front and index by id instead of object identity.

findings.title: Louvain node-removal state never restored when node stays in community
findings.description: In relaxedCommunities, `communityDegrees[current] -= degrees[index]` removes the node's degree from its current community before evaluating candidates, and `communityDegrees[best] += degrees[index]` re-adds it after. However, the initial `bestGain` is computed against the already-decremented `communityDegrees[current]`, while candidate loop also includes `current` in `candidates` and recomputes its gain identically — this is fine. The real issue: `labels[index] = best` is assigned unconditionally, but `weightByCommunity` is built from neighbor labels that can include stale community IDs after prior merges within the same pass; more importantly, `degrees[index] === 0` nodes are skipped entirely, so their communityDegrees contributions are never re-evaluated, and if all nodes are skipped the singleton labels stand — acceptable. The concrete bug is subtler: since `candidates` includes `current`, `bestGain` is computed twice for `current` (once as initialization, once in the loop) with the tie-break `candidate < best`; because `best` is initialized to `current`, a candidate with equal gain and lower index will replace it, but a candidate with equal gain evaluated when `best` has already moved to a lower index cannot be compared against communities not in `weightByCommunity`. This makes label assignment order-dependent across passes rather than deterministic in all cases.
findings.suggestedFix: Initialize `best = current; bestGain = -Infinity` and let the candidate loop (which already includes `current`) compute all gains uniformly, keeping the deterministic `candidate < best` tie-break.

findings.title: relaxedEdgeDensity uses adjacency mutated by community/2-core filtering with pre-split groups
findings.description: In agreementClusters, `indexes` maps the original group array references to indices, and `adjacency` is mutated (edges removed) by the community filter. Later, `coreClusters` are built from components that were run through `splitCompatibleChains`, which re-sorts and partitions groups. `relaxedEdgeDensity(component, indexes, adjacency)` is then computed on the split sub-cluster. Because the density is computed over the split component's size but the adjacency still reflects edges to groups that were split into other sub-clusters, an incompatible-claims split can leave a sub-cluster whose internal edges were removed only by community filtering — edges between now-separated sub-clusters are still present in `adjacency` and counted only when both endpoints are in the same component, so density can be understated for legitimately corroborated splits (edges to split-away peers no longer count toward the denominator's numerator), causing a corroborated cluster to be misclassified as uncorroborated.
findings.suggestedFix: Recompute relaxed edges among the members of each split component directly (via relaxedLocationWeight) instead of consulting the pre-split adjacency structure.

findings.title: 2-core peeling decrements degree of already-removed neighbors' peers incorrectly
findings.description: The peeling loop iterates `for (const neighbor of adjacency[index]!)` and decrements `degree[neighbor]` only when `inCore[neighbor]` is still true. However, when a node is enqueued multiple times (a node's degree can drop below 2 while it is already in the queue from an earlier decrement), the `if (!inCore[index]) continue;` guard handles re-processing. The actual bug: `degree` is initialized from `adjacency` AFTER community-edge deletion, but the deletion loop `adjacency[i]!.delete(j)` removes only the i→j direction when iterating `adjacency[i]`; since both directions are checked (`communities[i] !== communities[j]` is symmetric and both i and j iterate), symmetry holds. What does not hold: nodes with degree exactly 0 (isolated singletons) are enqueued and marked `inCore=false`, then reported as fringe components — intended. No functional issue found here on closer inspection of symmetry; however, a node appearing twice in `queue` after `inCore` was already set false is skipped, so the loop is safe. Downgrading: the real risk is that `degree[neighbor]!--` can push a neighbor into the queue multiple times, growing `queue` unboundedly relative to node count is bounded by edge count — acceptable. This finding flags the fragility for maintainers: duplicate queue entries make `queue.length` up to O(E), and the loop relies on the `inCore` guard for correctness.
findings.suggestedFix: Guard enqueueing with a check that the neighbor is not already queued below the threshold, or track queued state explicitly for clarity.

findings.title: indexes Map keyed by array reference breaks after splitCompatibleChains re-sorts
findings.description: `agreementClusters` reassigns `groups = [...groups].sort(...)` at the top, then builds `indexes` from the sorted copies. `splitCompatibleChains` creates `ordered = [...component].sort(...)` — this preserves the inner group array references, so `indexes.get(...)` lookups still succeed. However, `relaxedEdgeDensity` calls `indexes.get(groups[i]!)!` with a non-null assertion; if any code path ever passes a group array not present in the map (e.g., after `collapseSameReviewer` produces new arrays upstream, or a future refactor clones groups), this throws or silently yields `adjacency[undefined]`. Currently `adjacency[indexes.get(...)!]!` with an undefined index would throw a TypeError at runtime. This is a latent crash bug hidden by non-null assertions with no validation.
findings.suggestedFix: Avoid non-null assertions: look up indices defensively and throw a descriptive error, or compute density directly from the group members without the identity-keyed map.

findings.title: attachmentEvidence with empty supporters yields Math.min of empty array = Infinity guard missing
findings.description: In mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters, `supports = evidence.map(item => item.support)` and `support: Math.min(...supports)`. If `candidateMembers` is non-empty this is fine, but the code guards `candidateMembers.length === 0` with `continue` before mapping — however `evidence` is computed per candidate member against the target, and if `candidateMembers` were empty (guarded) Math.min() would return Infinity, passing the `support >= CORROBORATED_ATTACHMENT_SUPPORT` filter and attaching an empty candidate. The guard exists, but after attachments are applied (`candidate.groups = []`), emptied candidates remain in `clusters` for subsequent rounds. In the next round, `candidateMembers.length === 0` skips them — OK. The actual issue: an emptied candidate cluster remains in `clusters` and is passed as a potential `target` in `.filter((target) => ... target.corroborated ...)`; emptied candidates are never corroborated so they're excluded. However, emptied clusters ARE still passed to the final `mergeAnchoredCommunities` only after filtering `groups.length > 0` — OK. Net remaining bug: `strength: evidence.reduce(...)` sums strengths even from members whose individual support is 0 (evidence returns {support:0, strength:0} — strength is 0 in that path, fine) — but attachmentEvidence can return support 0 with nonzero strength? No: strength is derived from supporters which is empty when returning early. The genuine defect here: when `anchorCount === 1 && supporters.size < CORROBORATED_SINGLE_ANCHOR_SUPPORT`, support is zeroed but `strength` still sums the supporters' similarities, inflating the ranked `strength` tie-breaker for a candidate that should contribute nothing.
findings.suggestedFix: When support is forced to 0 for the single-anchor case, also return strength 0: `if (anchorCount === 1 && supporters.size < CORROBORATED_SINGLE_ANCHOR_SUPPORT) return { support: 0, strength: 0 };`

findings.title: Batched attachments can attach the same candidate cluster to targets that were themselves attached
findings.description: Attachments are collected against a frozen snapshot, then applied in a loop: `target.groups.push(...candidate.groups); candidate.groups = [];`. If cluster A is scheduled to attach to cluster B, and cluster B (uncorroborated clusters are the only candidates, but B could be a candidate while also being a target only if corroborated — candidates are non-corroborated, targets are corroborated, so A→B where B is also a candidate is impossible). However, two different candidates C1 and C2 can attach to the same target T; that is fine. The real hazard: a candidate can appear as `candidate` in one attachment while its `groups` array reference was captured in `ranked` computations of others — after `candidate.groups = []` the earlier `target.groups.push(...candidate.groups)` uses the pre-emptied array only if apply order matches collection order. Since apply is sequential and each candidate appears at most once, the specific bug is order-sensitivity between rounds: round 2 recomputes over mutated state, but the loop bound `Math.min(clusters.length, CORROBORATED_MAX_ATTACHMENT_ROUNDS)` uses clusters.length which includes emptied clusters, harmless. Minor but real: emptied candidate clusters remain in `clusters` and are still iterated as candidates each round (guarded), and `mergedClusters` filtering happens only at the end — the intermediate rounds' `clustersShareFile` on emptied groups compares two empty file sets (`filesA.size === filesB.size` → 0 === 0 → true) making `clustersShareFile` return true for empty candidates against any target with empty... no, target is corroborated and non-empty. Empty candidate: filesA is empty set, filesB non-empty → sizes differ → false. Guarded by candidateMembers.length check anyway. Downgraded to the ordering-sensitivity concern within mergeAnchoredCommunities calls.
findings.suggestedFix: Filter emptied clusters between rounds (`clusters = clusters.filter(c => c.groups.length > 0)`) to keep round semantics clear and avoid subtle empty-collection edge cases.

findings.title: mergeAnchoredCommunities mutates shared AgreementCluster objects across calls
findings.description: mergeAnchoredCommunities mutates `target.groups` in place and is called twice: once inside agreementClusters and once at the end of mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters on the same cluster objects. Because clusters are shared mutable objects, the second call operates on state already mutated by attachment rounds. Additionally, `remaining.sort(compareAgreementClusters)` is re-invoked after every merge inside the while loop, and `agreementClusterKey` depends on `chooseRepresentative` of the merged flat member list — the key of a merged cluster changes after each merge, so the `outer:` restart pattern re-sorts and rescans from scratch. This is O(n³ log n) worst case and, more importantly, the merged flag `corroborated` of the absorbed candidate is discarded: merging two corroborated clusters keeps target.corroborated true (fine), but if a fringe (non-corroborated) cluster was merged into groups via attachment, the final flatten treats the whole cluster as corroborated and collapses fringe members into the representative group — which appears intentional, but is undocumented and worth an explicit comment/test.
findings.suggestedFix: Document or assert the mutation contract; consider returning new cluster objects instead of mutating shared state between the two mergeAnchoredCommunities invocations.

findings.title: compatibleClaimKinds tests only titles for contract patterns, not descriptions
findings.description: TYPE_CONTRACT_PATTERN and the other regexes are applied to `a.title` / `b.title` only. A finding titled generically (e.g., 'Return value not fully typed') whose description says '@spec omits nil' will be classified as non-contract and can bridge into a runtime-nil cluster via the relaxed path — exactly the over-merge the guard is meant to prevent. The corpus test happens to pass because all typespec fixtures mention '@spec', 'typespec', or 'return type' in the title, but production titles are not guaranteed to.
findings.suggestedFix: Apply the contract-kind regexes to `${finding.title} ${finding.description}` (or title + first sentence of description) rather than title alone.

findings.title: Number.EPSILON is an inappropriate tolerance for modularity gain comparison
findings.description: The gain comparison uses `gain > bestGain + Number.EPSILON` and `Math.abs(gain - bestGain) <= Number.EPSILON`. Number.EPSILON (~2.2e-16) is the spacing of doubles near 1.0; gains here are sums/quotients of weights and can be much larger or smaller in magnitude, so the epsilon is effectively meaningless for values away from 1 (either always or never within tolerance). The module already defines CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON = 1e-9 for a similar purpose but doesn't use it here, so two mathematically-equal gains computed in different orders may fail the tie check and produce order-dependent community labels, undermining the determinism the test asserts.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a relative tolerance or the existing CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON: `if (gain > bestGain + CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON || (Math.abs(gain - bestGain) <= CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON && candidate < best))`.

findings.title: Double collapseSameReviewer may pick different representative than strict path
findings.description: collapseSameReviewer is applied once when building strictGroups and again after mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters. If the corroborated merge combines groups that each already collapsed the same reviewer (same model::role appearing in two merged groups), the second collapse must pick one member — the result depends on collapseSameReviewer's internal selection. This double-collapse changes which finding text survives for the representative compared to a single-pass collapse over all raw members, and can drop distinct findings from the same reviewer that were legitimately separate concepts pre-merge. If a merge is later judged wrong, the dropped member is unrecoverable in the output.
findings.suggestedFix: Collapse same-reviewer members only once, after the corroborated merge, or verify collapseSameReviewer is idempotent and order-independent with a test.

findings.title: conceptAnchors support threshold can exceed available reviewers for small clusters
findings.description: `support = Math.max(2, Math.ceil(reviewerCount * 0.4))`. For a 2-reviewer cluster, support = 2, meaning both reviewers must share the token — reasonable. But for reviewerCount = 1 (a fringe singleton cluster passed through mergeAnchoredCommunities or attachmentEvidence's conceptAnchors call on small clusters), support = 2 > 1, so anchors are always empty and `targetAnchors.size === 0` silently disables merging/attachment. In attachmentEvidence, an empty targetAnchors set means anchorCount is always 0 and every singleton attachment against small targets returns {0,0}. Since attachment targets must be corroborated (≥3 reviewers) this may be unreachable today, but mergeAnchoredCommunities is also invoked on fringe clusters where 1-reviewer clusters are common — those silently never merge via anchors, which may be intended but is not documented.
findings.suggestedFix: Document that single-reviewer clusters cannot produce anchors, or clamp support to reviewerCount when appropriate.

findings.title: corroborationFieldSimilar with two shared underscore-only tokens contradicts its comment
findings.description: The comment states 'A shared code identifier alone is only evidence that findings discuss the same function, not the same defect', yet the return allows `shared.length >= 2` where both shared tokens may be underscore identifiers (e.g., `trigger_label` and `column_name`). Two findings about two different defects in the same function that both reference the function name and a shared field name will pass this check, weakening the guard the comment claims. This is a logic/documentation mismatch that affects merge behavior.
findings.suggestedFix: Require at least one non-identifier token among shared tokens, or count underscore identifiers as at most one unit of evidence: `shared.some(t => !t.includes('_')) || shared.filter(t => !t.includes('_')).length + Math.min(1, shared.filter(t => t.includes('_')).length) >= 2`.

findings.title: relaxedLocationWeight recomputes similarity metrics already computed in the predicate
findings.description: relaxedLocationWeight calls relaxedLocationDuplicate (which computes jaccardSimilarity on titles and both field similarities) and then recomputes all three metrics. In agreementClusters this runs inside an O(n²) pairwise loop and again inside groupsRelaxedWeight's nested loops and mergeAnchoredCommunities' hasCrossEdge — the redundant tokenization is a measurable hot spot for large finding sets.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the three similarities once and derive both the boolean predicate and the weight from the same values; consider memoizing tokenization per finding.

findings.title: groupsShareLocation on empty groups vacuously returns true
findings.description: `a.every(...)` over an empty array returns true, so an empty group 'shares location' with anything, and clustersAreCompatible/clustersClaimsAreCompatible are likewise vacuously true for empty clusters. After attachment rounds set `candidate.groups = []`, emptied clusters flow into the final mergeAnchoredCommunities call only after a `groups.length > 0` filter, so today this is guarded — but the vacuous-truth behavior is a trap: any future caller passing an emptied cluster to clustersAreCompatible will get spurious compatibility and could merge unrelated clusters.
findings.suggestedFix: Return false (or throw) from groupsShareLocation/clustersAreCompatible when either side is empty.

findings.title: agreementClusterKey line-number padding breaks for negative or >10-digit lines
findings.description: `String(finding.startLine).padStart(10, '0')` produces lexicographically incorrect ordering for negative line numbers (the '-' sorts before digits inconsistently, e.g. '-000000001' vs '0000000002') and for pathological values exceeding 10 digits. Line numbers should never be negative, but there is no validation upstream in this diff; a defensive clamp or numeric comparison would remove the assumption.
findings.suggestedFix: Compare numerically in compareAgreementClusters instead of encoding numbers into a string key.

findings.title: Missing mustStaySeparate throws inside test instead of failing fixture validation
findings.description: When `miningProxyOvermerged` is set without `mustStaySeparate`, the test throws an Error mid-test after already running deduplicateFindings. This reports as a test failure with a generic message rather than a clear fixture-validation error, and the same check is duplicated in both tests. A malformed fixture is a corpus authoring error that should fail fast in a dedicated validation step (like the fixture sanity checks presumably at the top of the file).
findings.suggestedFix: Validate the fixture shape once when loading the corpus (before the describe blocks), or use a type-level discriminated union so miningProxyOvermerged implies mustStaySeparate.

findings.title: excludedTitles asserted absent from holding group but not asserted present elsewhere
findings.description: The positive-case assertion checks `heldTitles` does not contain each excluded title, but never asserts the excluded finding exists in the output at all. If dedup dropped an excluded finding entirely (a different bug), the test would still pass, silently weakening the over-merge guard. The later ao-7536-specific test does assert existence via `expect(excludedGroup).toBeDefined()`, but only for that one case.
findings.suggestedFix: In the generic positive-case test, also assert each excluded title appears in some group: `expect(groups.some(g => g.members.some(m => m.finding.title === excluded))).toBe(true)`.

findings.title: Attachment requires every candidate member to support the target (Math.min), including zero-evidence members
findings.description: `support: Math.min(...supports)` requires every member of a multi-member fringe component to independently clear the attachment evidence bar. A fringe component of two findings where one is a strong match and the other a weak paraphrase (support 0) will never attach, even though the comment says multi-member components are absorbed 'when every member supports the same target'. That is consistent with the comment, but combined with the tie-skip logic (`continue` when ranked[0] and ranked[1] tie on support, strength, and size), a legitimate attachment can be silently skipped forever since rounds are capped at 2 and ties are re-evaluated against nearly identical state each round. There is no logging or telemetry for skipped attachments, making production tuning of the calibrated thresholds blind.
findings.suggestedFix: Emit debug telemetry (or return diagnostics) for skipped attachments due to ties or min-support failures, to make threshold calibration observable.

findings.title: corroborationTokens filters tokens of length 1, dropping meaningful single-char identifiers
findings.description: `token.length > 1` drops single-character tokens. For most prose this is right, but code identifiers like `i`, `n` in 'n + 1' contexts are dropped — note PERFORMANCE_CONTRACT_PATTERN explicitly matches 'n + 1', so the token filter and the regex disagree about whether such fragments carry signal. Harmless today since the patterns run on raw text, but worth a comment to prevent future unification from changing behavior.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a brief comment noting the intentional divergence between regex-based claim-kind detection (raw text) and token-based similarity (filtered tokens).

findings.title: Community optimization omits the singleton-community option
findings.description: After removing a node from its current community, the Louvain step only considers neighboring community labels and the node's previous label. If reinserting it into every considered community has negative gain, leaving it in a new singleton community has gain zero and is the correct choice, but that option is unavailable. The implementation can therefore retain a weak bridge in an existing community or move it to a less-negative community, undermining the community boundary intended to prevent unrelated findings from being merged.
findings.suggestedFix: Include a fresh singleton community as a zero-gain candidate after removing each node. Select another community only when its insertion gain exceeds zero; otherwise assign the node to the singleton label. Maintain the new label's degree in `communityDegrees`, preferably using a map or dynamically allocated label.

findings.title: corroborationFieldSimilar contradicts its own identifier guard
findings.description: The comment states 'A shared code identifier alone is only evidence that findings discuss the same function, not the same defect within that function', and the code enforces this via `shared.some((token) => !token.includes('_'))`. However the fallback `|| shared.length >= 2` allows two shared tokens that both contain underscores (e.g. `trigger_label` and `column_name`) to establish a semantic edge purely on shared identifiers. Two findings about different defects in the same function will typically share multiple identifier tokens, so this fallback re-opens exactly the false-edge path the comment says must be prevented. Either drop the `shared.length >= 2` clause or filter underscore tokens from it.
findings.suggestedFix: return shared.some((token) => !token.includes('_')); // or: shared.filter(t => !t.includes('_')).length >= 1 || shared.length >= 2 with at least one non-identifier token

findings.title: Louvain gain comparison uses stale weightByCommunity for current community
findings.description: In relaxedCommunities, weightByCommunity is built from neighbor labels before the node is removed from its community, which is correct, but the initial bestGain for `current` is computed with `(weightByCommunity.get(current) ?? 0)` while candidate gains reuse the same map. If the node has a self-referential label collision (label equals its own index and a neighbor also carries that label index after prior moves), the weight to 'current' can include edges to nodes that have since moved out, because labels are node indices and community identity is not tracked separately. This is a known fragility of label-as-index Louvain: after node X moves into community Y, communityDegrees is keyed by label but weightByCommunity for later nodes aggregates by current labels, so it stays consistent — however isolated nodes (degree 0) are skipped and never re-labeled, leaving singleton labels that later nodes can join based on a communityDegrees entry that only reflects the isolated node's zero degree. Joining a zero-degree 'community' label gives gain 0 - 0 = 0 and can tie with the current community, with the tie broken by smaller label index, causing non-obvious label churn. Consider filtering candidate labels to communities with positive degree or explicitly excluding degree-0 labels.
findings.suggestedFix: Skip candidates whose communityDegrees[candidate] === 0 when candidate !== current, or relabel communities compactly after each pass.

findings.title: Non-null assertion c! bypasses strict null checks
findings.description: The over-merge guard test uses `c!.expected.excludedTitles` with a non-null assertion. Per the project's TypeScript review conventions ('non-null assertions (!) without validation'), this should be guarded — if the corpus lookup fails the test would crash with an unhelpful TypeError instead of a clear assertion message.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `expect(c).toBeDefined()` (or an early throw) before dereferencing, then use `c.expected` directly.

findings.title: Test hard-codes combinedSimilarity threshold coupling
findings.description: `expect(combinedSimilarity(variants[0]!, variants[1]!)).toBeLessThan(0.3)` hard-codes the current strict-threshold value (0.3) as a magic number. If the strict jaccardThreshold is retuned, this precondition assertion silently becomes meaningless or fails for the wrong reason. Reference the threshold constant or add a comment tying 0.3 to the strict dedup threshold.
findings.suggestedFix: Import the threshold constant used by deduplicateFindings and assert against it, e.g. toBeLessThan(jaccardThreshold).

findings.title: Louvain community-degree indexing assumes labels are valid array indexes
findings.description: In relaxedCommunities, `communityDegrees` is indexed by community label (`communityDegrees[current]`, `communityDegrees[candidate]`). Labels start as node indexes so this works initially, but as nodes move between communities, labels remain within [0, count) so array bounds hold. However, when a node moves out of community X and X becomes empty, `communityDegrees[X]` may become a small residual and later comparisons against that stale empty community can produce spurious gains, plus floating-point subtraction can leave tiny negative residues in `communityDegrees` that bias tie-breaking. More importantly, the algorithm never renumbers labels, so the deterministic tie-break `candidate < best` depends on the arbitrary initial ordering of groups; combined with the pre-sort by `agreementClusterKey` this is deterministic, but if two findings share identical file/lines/title, the key falls back to `finding.id`, which is model-generated and not guaranteed unique across reviews — identical keys would make ordering (and thus community assignment) depend on input array order.
findings.suggestedFix: Clamp `communityDegrees` values at 0 after removal, and include a guaranteed-unique component (e.g., the TaggedFinding's model::role) in agreementClusterKey so sorting is a total order independent of input order.

findings.title: conceptAnchors support threshold uses reviewer count of the whole cluster
findings.description: `support = Math.max(2, Math.ceil(reviewerCount * 0.4))` scales with cluster size, but `distinctReviewers(groups)` counts reviewers in the cluster being anchored. For a singleton fringe cluster (1 reviewer), support floor is 2, so conceptAnchors of a singleton is always empty (a single reviewer can never supply 2 distinct reviewer assignments per token). This means `mergeAnchoredCommunities` can never merge a fringe singleton via anchors (`targetAnchors.size === 0 || candidateAnchors.size === 0` always short-circuits), and in `attachmentEvidence` only the target's anchors matter — but any two-member fringe cluster where both members are the same model::role also yields zero anchors. If that's intended (single-reviewer clusters shouldn't self-corroborate), it deserves a comment; otherwise fringe merging silently never happens for these cases.
findings.suggestedFix: Either document that single-reviewer clusters intentionally produce no anchors, or lower the floor to 1 for clusters with fewer than 2 distinct reviewers if fringe-to-fringe anchor merging is desired.

findings.title: Simultaneous attachment can attach the same evidence twice and mutate shared targets
findings.description: In mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters, all attachments in a round are computed against frozen state and then applied. However, two different candidates may attach to two different targets that are later merged, or a candidate could be chosen as `target` reference while another candidate in the same round attaches into it — the code pushes `candidate.groups` into `target.groups` for each attachment, but if the same `candidate` object appears as a `target` for another attachment (impossible since targets must be corroborated and candidates are not — OK), the real issue is that after `target.groups.push(...candidate.groups)`, the target's anchor set and evidence change, yet subsequent rounds recompute from mutated state as documented. The subtle bug: `candidate.groups = []` empties the candidate, but the candidate cluster object remains in `clusters` and is re-evaluated in the next round with `candidateMembers.length === 0`, which is skipped — fine. The actual defect is `Math.min(...supports)` when `candidateMembers` is empty returns `Infinity`, but that path is guarded. However, if a candidate has multiple members and only some have support, `Math.min` requires EVERY member to individually reach CORROBORATED_ATTACHMENT_SUPPORT — supports of 0 from one member veto the whole component even when the component was formed by transitive weak edges; this is stated as intended in the comment, but `Math.min(...supports)` on a large array can also hit argument-length limits for very large components (spread of thousands of elements).
findings.suggestedFix: Use `supports.reduce((m, v) => Math.min(m, v), Infinity)` instead of spreading into Math.min to avoid call-argument limits on large components.

findings.title: mergeAnchoredCommunities merges corroborated clusters without re-checking density/reviewers
findings.description: When two corroborated clusters are merged, the merged cluster keeps `corroborated: true` implicitly (the target's flag), but the merged whole is never re-validated against CORROBORATED_MIN_REVIEWERS or CORROBORATED_MIN_DENSITY. More significantly, after attachment (`mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters` second pass), fringe clusters absorbed into a corroborated target inherit its corroborated status and are flattened into one group at the end — a fringe cluster that never met the 2-core requirement is merged into the final group as full members. That is the design intent for attachment, but in `mergeAnchoredCommunities` two *non-corroborated* clusters are never merged (guarded), while a corroborated + non-corroborated pair is also skipped — only corroborated pairs merge. The gap: the cross-edge check requires only ONE pair with `relaxedLocationWeight > 0` between two clusters that may each contain many groups; a single weak lexical edge between large clusters merges everything, potentially undoing the community split that relaxedCommunities performed on exactly those edges (the anchor+edge test can re-bridge communities that Louvain deliberately separated).
findings.suggestedFix: When re-merging communities that Louvain split, require stronger evidence than a single positive-weight edge — e.g., a minimum number of cross edges or a minimum aggregate cross-weight proportional to cluster sizes.

findings.title: O(n^2) re-sort inside merge loop; quadratic-times-n behavior on large clusters
findings.description: After each merge, `remaining.sort(compareAgreementClusters)` re-sorts the whole array and restarts the outer loop from scratch (`break outer` with `merged = true`). Each merge costs O(n log n) sort plus O(n^2) pair scanning with expensive `clustersAreCompatible` (which is itself O(members^4) via nested every/every/every/every). With many findings at the same location this can become a noticeable hot spot. Also, `agreementClusterKey` is recomputed via `chooseRepresentative` on every comparison during sort.
findings.suggestedFix: Cache cluster keys, only re-insert the merged cluster at its sorted position, and continue scanning rather than restarting the full O(n^2) pass after each merge.

findings.title: Regex patterns are anchored to English keywords and miss common synonyms
findings.description: TYPE_CONTRACT_PATTERN matches '@spec', 'typespec(s)', 'return type' but not 'spec is too narrow', 'dialyzer', 'type signature', or 'return value type'. PERFORMANCE_CONTRACT_PATTERN matches 'n + 1' with flexible spacing but misses 'N+1 query' written as 'n plus one' or 'select n+1' variants are covered — however 'missing index' requires the literal word order 'missing ... index' and misses 'index is missing' or 'no index on'. Because compatibleClaimKinds returns false when only ONE side matches a pattern, an asymmetric wording (one title says 'return type', the other says 'type signature') will block a legitimate merge — the guard is one-directional in effect and sensitive to phrasing. This is a calibrated heuristic, but the incomplete keyword lists will produce both false blocks and false passes on real corpora.
findings.suggestedFix: Broaden patterns (e.g., add \btype signature\b, \bdialyzer\b, \bindex (is )?missing\b) or derive claim kinds from the taxonomy/concepts already extracted by extractConcepts instead of ad-hoc regexes.

findings.title: corroborationFieldSimilar treats any token containing '_' as a code identifier
findings.description: The heuristic `shared.some((token) => !token.includes('_')) || shared.length >= 2` assumes underscore implies code identifier. Snake_case words in prose (e.g., copied variable names is intended) are fine, but camelCase and PascalCase identifiers (common in TypeScript/JS findings: `getUserData`, `myFunc`) contain no underscore and will count as a normal semantic token, creating exactly the false semantic edge the comment says it's guarding against. In a TS/JS codebase, a single shared camelCase function name across two unrelated findings satisfies the check.
findings.suggestedFix: Also treat tokens matching /[a-z][A-Z]/ (camelCase) or tokens that appear in backticks in the source text as identifiers, or check tokens against identifiers extracted from the diff hunk.

findings.title: relaxedEdgeDensity computed against pre-community-filtered adjacency after splitCompatibleChains
findings.description: `coreClusters` computes density using the `indexes` map keyed by original group array references and the `adjacency` structure that was filtered to intra-community edges. However, `splitCompatibleChains` can split a component into multiple clusters; density for each sub-cluster is then computed over only that sub-cluster's pairs but against adjacency that includes edges to groups no longer in the sub-cluster — actually only pairs within the sub-cluster are counted, so edges leaving the sub-cluster are ignored, which deflates density. A component split into chains may fail CORROBORATED_MIN_DENSITY purely due to the split even though the original component was dense. Conversely, `distinctReviewers` is checked on the sub-cluster, which is correct. The interaction between chain-splitting and density gating is untested.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute density before splitting (per component) or recompute adjacency restricted to the sub-cluster and document which is intended; add a test covering a dense component that splitCompatibleChains partitions.

findings.title: collapseSameReviewer applied twice; second pass can change the representative
findings.description: Strict groups are built with collapseSameReviewer, then mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters flattens clusters and collapseSameReviewer runs again on merged members. If the same model::role contributed findings to two different strict groups that later merge, the second collapse will drop one of them — that's presumably intended. But the strict-path behavior changed: previously chooseRepresentative was picked per strict group; now for unmerged clusters the same members flow through, which should be identity, EXCEPT that mergeCorroboratedLocationClusters may reorder members via sorting inside agreementClusters, so chooseRepresentative could pick a different representative for previously stable groups if it is order-sensitive. If chooseRepresentative has any order-dependent tie-breaking, existing group representatives may silently change for untouched groups.
findings.suggestedFix: Verify chooseRepresentative is fully order-independent, or preserve original member order for clusters that were not merged.

findings.title: CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON unused for support/size ties and duplicated by localeCompare fallback
findings.description: The ambiguity check compares support and size with exact equality and strength within CORROBORATED_TIE_EPSILON, then skips attachment. But the sort's final tie-break is `a.key.localeCompare(b.key)` — localeCompare is locale-sensitive and can order differently across Node ICU builds/locales, making the 'unambiguous top candidate' selection environment-dependent when strength differs by more than epsilon but keys decide ordering. Since keys only decide ordering when support/strength/size all tie — which is exactly the case the guard skips — this is mostly moot, but the guard doesn't cover the case where sizes differ but strength and support tie; then order between #1 and #2 is decided by size, which is a weak proxy for correctness of attachment.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a non-locale-sensitive comparison (e.g., `a.key < b.key ? -1 : ...`) for determinism across environments.

findings.title: Stopword list is English-only and duplicates may exist with base STOPWORDS
findings.description: CORROBORATION_STOPWORDS extends STOPWORDS with English auxiliaries and generic nouns. Model reviews in other languages (or codebases with non-English identifiers) won't benefit from stopword removal, inflating token overlap and making the 0.20/0.10 thresholds behave differently. Also 'missing', 'no', 'not' being stopwords means negation is stripped: 'does not validate X' and 'validates X' share the same corroboration tokens (hasOpposingSentiment presumably guards this, but the tokenizer itself erases polarity).
findings.suggestedFix: Document the English-only assumption, and confirm hasOpposingSentiment fully covers negation since corroborationTokens strips it.

findings.title: Characterization layer deleted; corpus schema violations now fail at runtime mid-test
findings.description: The new branch throws `new Error(...)` inside the test body when `mustStaySeparate` is missing on a `miningProxyOvermerged` case, but only after calling deduplicateFindings — wasted work and the guard runs twice (once per test). Also `mustStaySeparate` is typed as a required tuple check at runtime but optional in the interface; a corpus file with `miningProxyOvermerged: true` and no `mustStaySeparate` produces two confusing runtime errors instead of a schema validation failure in the fixture-loading `it` block that presumably validates corpus shape.
findings.suggestedFix: Validate the miningProxyOvermerged/mustStaySeparate invariant once at corpus load time (in the existing schema-check describe block), and check before running deduplicateFindings.

findings.title: Negative-guard test assumes each mustStaySeparate title lands in exactly one group
findings.description: `groups.find(...)` returns the FIRST group containing the title. If dedup ever duplicates a finding across groups (a regression this suite should catch), `leftGroup !== rightGroup` could pass spuriously while the same title also appears in the other group. Similarly the 'independent agreement' test checks only the first matching group's reviewer-pair ratio.
findings.suggestedFix: Use `groups.filter(...)` and assert exactly one group holds each title before comparing identity.

findings.title: Determinism test only permutes review order, not intra-review finding order
findings.description: The determinism test reverses the review array but each review contains a single finding. The new code paths (sorting by agreementClusterKey which can collide on identical file/lines/title/id, Louvain label tie-breaking, attachment ranking) have order sensitivity primarily across findings within reviews and across duplicate keys. A stronger test would shuffle findings with identical titles/locations and multiple findings per review.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a determinism test with multiple findings per review, including two findings with identical file/startLine/endLine/title from different models, permuted in several orders.

findings.title: attachmentEvidence mixes singleton description+fix tokens against title-only cluster anchors
findings.description: conceptAnchors builds anchors from member TITLES only, but the singleton's anchor set is built from title + description + suggestedFix concatenated. This asymmetry makes attachment much easier for singletons with verbose descriptions: any two words from the singleton's description that happen to match cluster title anchors satisfy `anchorCount >= 2`, even if the singleton's title is about something else. Combined with CORROBORATED_ATTACHMENT_THRESHOLD of 0.12 (a low combined-similarity bar), a wordy but unrelated finding at the same lines can attach to a corroborated cluster and inherit consensus it did not earn — inflating the group's agreement ratio used for minConsensusScore.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute singleton anchors from the title only (matching conceptAnchors), or require at least one anchor to come from the singleton's title.
